items.title: Syfy's 4-Season Masterpiece Is A Rare Example Of A TV Remake Beating The Movie
items.summary: Remakes and reboots have a bad reputation. Many have angered their source material's fanbase, who often criticize the result for appearing to trade creativity for a profit, while others have missed the point of the original. It is relatively rare for a sci-fi remake to be better than the original, but when a production reflects the spirit of the source material while further expanding its world, it can capture lightning in a bottle. This approach made a remake of a cult Brad Pitt movie into one of TV's best time travel shows , despite the series reinterpreting the original movie.
items.t: Syfy's 4-Season Masterpiece Is A Rare Example Of A TV Remake Beating The Movie

items.title: 12-Episode Prime Video Masterpiece Is A Rare Show Where Every Line Is Perfect
items.summary: Very few TV shows are perfect from start to finish, but an inordinate number of classic British sitcoms are, because they’ve figured out the trick: don’t do too many seasons or episodes. If you only do a handful of episodes, then it’ll be a lot easier to stick the landing. It was much easier for Ricky Gervais and Stephen Mercant to make 14 perfect episodes of the original British Office than it was for the American remake to churn out more episodes than that every single year, for a grand total of more than 200.

items.title: Russell Crowe’s Classic Thriller Is Still His Greatest Movie 27 Years Later
items.summary: Between 1997 and 1999, Russell Crowe became an international superstar. His measured intensity and knack for disappearing into a role put him on the radar of critics, especially when played several uber-slick, violent characters in Virtuosity , The Quick and the Dead , and LA Confidential . Then, shortly before he nailed the role of a sword-and-sandals picture action hero in perennial dad-cinema favorite Gladiator , Crowe truly disappeared into his greatest performance: Big tobacco whistleblower Jeffrey Wigand . In Michael Mann's obsessively detailed true corruption story The Insider , Crowe showed a new side of himself in a character completely at the mercy of the powers that be. His portrayal of Wigand is schlubby, pasty, and paranoid — everything his prior high-profile roles were not.
items.t: Russell Crowe’s Classic Thriller Is Still His Greatest Movie 27 Years Later

items.title: This 106-Minute James Bond Thriller Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Paramount+
items.summary: The James Bond franchise was at a crossroads before the decision to hire Daniel Craig to play the iconic spy. While Pierce Brosnan ’s tenure was prolific (especially compared to the glacial pace of the Craig films’ release schedule), the series had largely veered into the world of unfashionable (at the time) wacky camp by its 2002 finale, Die Another Day , and the character was in need of a refresh, like Batman after 1997’s Batman and Robin . And like 2005’s Batman Begins , Craig’s first outing, Casino Royale , was a tightly focused origin story that put the character in a grim pressure cooker that would teach him the tools of the trade. But unlike Batman Begins ’ all-timer follow-up, Casino Royale’s sequel Quantum of Solace was a mixed bag at best, widely criticized for squandering the first film’s setup in favor of a generic spy thriller. Whether that reputation is deserved is up for debate, but its upcoming departure from Paramount+ on Novemner 19, 2026, should encourage a second look.
items.t: This 106-Minute James Bond Thriller Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Paramount+

items.title: Heartland review – Jessica Chastain’s Netflix country music thriller is more miss than hit
items.summary:
The Oscar winner plays a singer turned detective searching for her niece in an overly generic Nashville-based mystery that fails to find its footing

Given the popularity of its music and the streaming services’ interest in faith-based programming, I’m always a little surprised that there aren’t more movies and TV shows about Nashville. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. There are plenty of enduring contradictions to mine there – the hyper-masculine men singing with their hearts on their sleeve, the Madonna-badass complex among its relatively few female stars, the suburban money in a genre ostensibly speaking to the rural common man.

Netflix seems to be aiming for some of those complexities with Heartland, a patchy neo-noir thriller starring Jessica Chastain as a washed-up former star turned vigilante detective with an axe to grind on Music Row. Chastain’s Misty Jones is certainly a thorny Nashville archetype, a female lead we might call “unlikable” painted in the stark terms of a bad country song (said with love as someone raised on country radio). items.title: ‘Women are pitted against each other. It’s a bloodsport’: Billie Piper on industry infighting, Elsinore’s Oscar buzz and thriving on personal crisis
items.summary:
The teen pop star turned Olivier-winning actor stars as Andrew Scott’s best friend in the acclaimed Ian Charleson biopic. She talks kindred spirits, social media and trying to channel a ‘mad storm of grief’

The late Billie Whitelaw, whom Samuel Beckett considered “a perfect actress”, was on stage in the middle of rehearsals one day when she asked the playwright: “Where should I be looking?” To which Beckett replied: “Inwards.”

Hearing this story, another Billie – the teen pop star turned Doctor Who companion and Olivier award-winning powerhouse Billie Piper – lets out a laugh so raucous and expansive, it is as if a flock of gaily coloured birds has been released into the room, flapping and squawking in every corner. “Fuck, that’s awesome,” she says.

items.title: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past
items.summary:
The latest film version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol is decent enough, though its star is rather better as the legendary miser before redemption arrives

Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Christmas Eve by the appearance of three Christmas ghosts, from yuletides past, present and future. It sticks to the accepted narrative beats and more or less all the familiar episodes, but with a few twists.

Continue reading...
items.t: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past

items.title: ‘Goats are good. They listen’: the herder who defeated Montenegro’s military – and can identify her cows’ herby burps
items.summary:
To Hold a Mountain tells the incredible story of a woman whose way of life was threatened when she heard her pastures were set to become a Nato training zone

The star of To Hold a Mountain is having trouble with her goats, which keep escaping. So my interview with Mileva “Gara” Jovanović is rescheduled to a moment where the animals are under control and Gara can descend from the peaks to her small winter residence in a small village near the capital of Podgorica, for a video call.

“You have to take care of them because they are always searching for their paths,” says Gara, whose Montenegrin is translated into English by Biljana Tutorov, the joint writer-director of the stunning film about Gara’s life in the mountains of Sinjajevina. “But the goats are good, especially when they know the shepherdess. I’m a good shepherdess. They listen to me.”

items.title: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp
items.summary:
The It Follows and Longlegs star tears into the role of a murderous governess in this hit-and-miss adaptation of Virginia Feito’s gory novel

It’s not that hard to figure out why a lower-class woman toiling away in Victorian England would be so easily driven to violently murder everyone around her. If it’s not the brittle entitlement of those who employ you, it’s the unending misogyny of the system you’re forced to be a subservient part of, all the while being underpaid and undervalued and at the mercy of sexual violence, a multitude of diseases and an average lifespan of just 42.

As Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe) fills the frame in Victorian Psycho, heading to a new job as governess for a rich family, it’s easy to be on her side. Even as her murderous impulses start to rear their head, they’re made somewhat understandable, although Winifred isn’t just a woman reacting to the various injustices of the time – she’s one responding to a demon within her, a darkness she has chosen to embrace rather than resist. Darkness is her friend, a protection against harm, and a way to possess some sort of control in a world that has denied her any of it.

Continue reading...
items.t: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp

items.title: ‘I trusted a lot of people, and the wrong people, and I shouldn’t have’: Charlotte Kirk on navigating Hollywood
items.summary:
The British actor took up writing and producing to have control over what she stars in after a scandal involving some of the most powerful men in the film business

After a recent run as an assassin, a serial killer and a gangster, Charlotte Kirk was looking for something a little lighter, and surely nothing can be more jolly, more wholesome than a Christmas romcom. In Christmas & Chaos, Kirk plays Sadie, a pop star in search of a hit – or, to be more precise, three hits for a new musical by an impresario (a comedic Jason Isaacs who only appears on screen via video call). She has just a couple of weeks to come up with something with handsome-and-heartbroken composer (Ben McGregor).

Kirk, who also produced the film, approached Jamie Adams, director of several low-budget British films, including Black Mountain Poets, intrigued by his regular use of improvisation. They worked out the story together, says Kirk, but made it without a script. All they knew was that “this was a Christmas movie, these two have got a deadline to make these hit songs and maybe there’ll be some kind of romance. And then it became something else, which is even more interesting.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I trusted a lot of people, and the wrong people, and I shouldn’t have’: Charlotte Kirk on navigating Hollywood

items.title: Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas review – Netflix unloads more slapdash festive fare
items.summary:
Incompetent direction almost kills the Christmas spirit but American Idol winner Fantasia Barrino Taylor brings down the house

Thanksgiving is right around the corner, which means Christmas creep is in full effect and the floodgates holding back the seasonal tide of holiday movies have opened to fully drown yuletide junkies in cheer. Among the first out of the gates is Netflix’s The Gospel of Christmas, brought to you by the maker of A Madea Christmas.

Instead of Tyler Perry in drag, reluctantly upholding the role of family linchpin, this time it’s Durrell Babbs – AKA the R&B stalwart Tank – playing Isaac, a secular musician who is forced into ministry when his pastor father charges him with resurrecting a sister congregation that’s become a blight in a New York neighborhood defined by immorality and anomie. (East New York, maybe.) The 103-minute feature is both a ploy to horn in on Hallmark’s well-established territory and a proper return to Perry’s roots in gospel musical theater – but with considerably more money behind it and greater latitude to bend the usual chestnuts on faith and family toward his Old Testament-facing sermons.

items.t: Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas review – Netflix unloads more slapdash festive fare

items.title: How to Rob a Bank review – Amazon’s anti-capitalist caper is far from a riot
items.summary:
Nicholas Hoult, Anna Sawai and Pete Davidson play Robin Hood in this simple-minded and unexciting attempt to mix social commentary with action

In case you were somehow blissfully unaware, America is in a very dark place and Americans are not very happy about it. Last week’s midterms saw a historic blue wave propelled by the high cost of living and the low trust in those making decisions, but restoring any small shred of faith in the system and any vague semblance of financial equity is still unlikely to come anytime soon.

It’s therefore theoretically ideal timing for films that provide some sort of rousing David v Goliath catharsis, a win on-screen when one feels entirely out of reach in real life. But like Paul Greengrass’s muddy and muddled peasant revolt drama The Uprising which crashed and burned in September, David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank can’t quite find a way to capture a moment that should be easy to capture. The director is best known for synthetic action films that prioritise noise above all else, from Deadpool 2 to Bullet Train to Hobbs & Shaw, a tonal throughline that could be most generously described as “annoying”.

items.t: How to Rob a Bank review – Amazon’s anti-capitalist caper is far from a riot

items.title: Soul Patrol review – heartstopping story of the US army’s first Black special ops team at work in Vietnam
items.summary:
Based on a 2003 memoir, this remarkable documentary shows the incredible bravery these young men showed in the face of battle and unrelenting bigotry

Here is the remarkable story of the US army’s “Soul Patrol” unit in the Vietnam war: the all-Black Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol (or LURP), a six-man team of largely teenage African American soldiers, within Company F 51st Infantry. Their duty was to go behind the Vietcong enemy lines, each carrying 150lbs of kit and an M16 assault rifle, and in conditions of terrifying danger report on the enemy’s movements. One heart stopping anecdote is about a panicky member of the unit, who had never seen fireflies before, and became convinced he had seen a Vietcong insurgent in the undergrowth, smoking a cigarette. The film also reports on their later, poignant reunion as old men, using their contemporary home-movie footage and dramatically recreating some scenes.

It is based on the 2003 memoir of the same title by unit member Ed Emanuel (who had gone into journalism in civilian life), based on his own experiences and those of his comrades who he had been able to track down. The publication of the book itself was intended to bring other ex-soldiers out of the woodwork, which it duly did. The Soul Patrol was at one level a special forces unit, an elite squad that was tough, capable, resourceful, operating at the highest standards of soldiering – and yet it was also subject to racist exploitation as cannon-fodder. This was what many in the unit came to suspect, and one interviewee here recounts his almost hallucinatory…
items.t: Soul Patrol review – heartstopping story of the US army’s first Black special ops team at work in Vietnam

items.title: Donnie Dunagan, original voice of Disney’s Bambi and triple Purple Heart marine, dies aged 92
items.summary:
Dunagan was six when he voiced the young deer in the classic cartoon, with an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died

Donnie Dunagan, who voiced Bambi in the Walt Disney classic, as well as playing the son of Frankenstein opposite Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff, has died aged 92.

Dunagan was six when he was chosen to provide the voice of the young deer in the animation’s most heartbreaking chapter. He recalled the experience in the recording booth as easy and relaxed, with rudimentary technology and notes from an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died when voicing Bambi’s reaction to his mother being killed by a hunter.

Continue reading...
items.t: Donnie Dunagan, original voice of Disney’s Bambi and triple Purple Heart marine, dies aged 92
